blocks.text: Once a prompt has a name and a set of arguments, a client still has real work to do before any of it reaches a model. It has to ask the server to fill in the template, hand the user a chance to look it over, and only then pass the result along to the LLM.

This lesson walks through that whole path. We will trace a single prompts/get call from the moment a user picks a slash command, through the filled message list the server hands back, to the preview and edit step many good clients build in before anything is sent.
By the end you should be able to write the client side code for this flow yourself, in either Python or JavaScript, and know exactly where a thoughtful client pauses to let a human stay in control.
1. What prompts/get Actually Returns

blocks.alt: A prompts get call returns a filled list of messages

blocks.text: A prompts/get call does not return a single string of text. It returns a small, structured result: a list of messages, each with a role and content, exactly the shape an LLM API expects for a conversation.
The server has already done the substitution work by the time this result reaches the client. Every placeholder in the template has been replaced with the argument values the client passed in.
2. Calling prompts/get With Filled In Arguments
The request side of this call is simple: a prompt name and an arguments object, where every key matches one of the argument names the prompt declared.
Every value in that object is a plain string, since prompt arguments never carry richer types than that.
3. Where the Argument Values Come From

A client rarely invents argument values on its own. Most of the time they come from a user typing them into a slash command, filling out a small form the client generated from the prompt's declared arguments.
Typing something like slash draft_apology_email Priya, a delayed refund, warm is what triggers the client to parse those words into named fields before ever calling prompts/get.
The prompt's own declared argument list, fetched earlier through prompts/list, is what tells the client which field each typed value maps to.

items: Positional words typed after a slash command name, matched to arguments in declared order
A small form the client renders, one field per declared argument
Values already present in the conversation, such as a customer name mentioned earlier
Sensible defaults the client applies for optional arguments a user skipped

blocks.text: 4. From a Slash Command to a Filled Request

blocks.alt: A slash command collecting arguments turns into a filled prompts get request

blocks.text: A slash command is really just a friendly interface sitting in front of prompts/get. The user experience is typing a short line of text, but underneath, the client is building the same structured arguments object every time.
5. Sending the Request and Reading the Response
Once the arguments object is built, the actual call is a routine JSON RPC request over whatever transport the client already has open to the server.

code.content:
async def fetch_prompt_messages(session, prompt_name, arguments):
    result = await session.get_prompt(name=prompt_name, arguments=arguments)
    return result.messages

blocks.text: The client does not need to know anything about how the server filled the template. It only needs the finished messages list that comes back.
6. The Anatomy of a Rendered Message List

A rendered prompt can return one message or several, and each one carries a role, almost always user or assistant, and content that is usually plain text but can also be an image or an embedded resource.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","What it holds"],"rows":[["role","Who the message is attributed to, typically user or assistant"],["content.type","text, image, or resource"],["content.text","The filled in text, present when content.type is text"],["content.resource","A reference to file or document content, when content.type is resource"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Feeding the Messages Into the LLM Call

blocks.alt: Rendered messages are fed directly into the LLM call

blocks.text: Because the messages already match the shape an LLM API expects, the client usually just appends them to whatever conversation it is already building and sends the whole thing along.
8. Why a Preview Step Matters

blocks.alt: A preview step lets the user see the final prompt before it is sent

blocks.text: A filled in prompt is still text a server assembled on the client's behalf, and the user typed the arguments quickly, possibly with a typo or a phrase that reads oddly once it lands inside the template.
Showing the rendered text before it goes anywhere near the model gives the user a last honest look at exactly what will be sent, not just what they typed into a form.

blocks.title: Trust through visibility
blocks.content: A user who can see the exact text a model is about to receive trusts the tool more, and catches mistakes before they turn into a wasted or embarrassing response.

blocks.text: 9. Letting the User Edit the Rendered Prompt

blocks.alt: A rendered prompt can be edited by the user before it is sent

blocks.text: Preview only becomes genuinely useful once a user can change what they see. A good client opens the rendered text in an editable field rather than a read only bubble.
Any edit the user makes should replace the content of the relevant message directly, with no need to re run prompts/get or touch the server again.
This keeps the flow fast, since a small wording tweak should never require another round trip to the server.
10. Implementing the Preview and Edit Step
Concretely, this means keeping the rendered messages in local editable state until the user confirms, rather than firing the LLM call the instant the server responds.
11. Handling Multiple Messages in a Preview
Some prompts return more than one message, perhaps a short user message paired with an earlier assistant turn meant to set up context.

A preview that only shows the first message and silently sends the rest unseen defeats the whole point of previewing at all, so every message in the list deserves its own visible, and ideally editable, slot.
Ordering also matters here, the messages should be shown and sent in exactly the order the server returned them.
12. Embedded Resources Inside Prompt Messages

blocks.alt: A prompt message can embed resource content directly inside it

blocks.text: Occasionally a rendered message carries a resource instead of plain text, a reference to a file or a document the prompt is meant to reason over.
A preview for this kind of message should show something meaningful, such as the resource name or a short excerpt, rather than an unreadable block of raw identifiers.
13. Handling a Failed prompts/get Call

blocks.alt: A failed prompts get call is surfaced as a clear error rather than a silent gap

blocks.text: Sometimes prompts/get fails, a required argument was missing, or the prompt name itself no longer exists on the server. The client should surface that failure clearly instead of silently sending nothing to the model.
A failed call should also leave the user's original slash command input intact, so they can fix it and try again without retyping everything.
14. Caching a Prompt Definition Without Caching the Render
A client can reasonably cache the prompt list from prompts/list, so it does not refetch names and argument definitions on every keystroke of a slash command.
The actual rendered result from prompts/get should not be cached the same way, since it depends on the specific arguments a user just typed and will differ almost every time.

blocks.title: Cache the shape, not the content
blocks.content: It is fine to remember what arguments a prompt needs. It is not fine to remember what a previous rendering said and reuse it for a new set of values.

blocks.text: 15. Slash Commands as the Common Trigger
Slash commands are the most familiar entry point into this whole flow because they map naturally onto a prompt's name and argument list, one word for the command, the rest for the values.

Nothing about prompts/get requires a slash command specifically. A client could just as easily trigger it from a button, a menu item, or an automated step, as long as it still collects the right arguments first.
Whatever the trigger, the argument collecting step and the prompts/get call underneath stay exactly the same.
16. Running the Same Prompt Again With New Values
Nothing stops a user from invoking the same slash command twice with different values. Each call is independent, its own prompts/get request and its own preview.
A client should never assume the previous rendered result is still valid once new arguments are typed in, it needs a fresh call every time.
17. Putting the Whole Flow Together
Start to finish, the flow is: collect arguments from the user, call prompts/get, receive the filled messages, show them for preview, accept any edits, then pass the final messages into the LLM call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Who does it"],"rows":[["Collect argument values","User, via slash command or form"],["Call prompts/get","Client"],["Fill the template","Server"],["Show a preview","Client"],["Approve or edit the text","User"],["Send to the LLM","Client"]]}

blocks.text: Worked Example
A user types slash draft_apology_email, Priya, a delayed refund, warm into their client. The client parses this into an arguments object and calls prompts/get.
The server returns a single filled user message. The client shows it in an editable box, the user adds one line asking for a small discount to be mentioned, then confirms.

code.content:
edited_text = rendered.messages[0].content.text + "\nPlease also mention a small discount on their next order."
final_messages = [{"role": "user", "content": edited_text}]
response = call_llm(model="the configured model", messages=final_messages)

blocks.text: Only after that final confirmed edit does anything reach the model, and the user saw the exact wording the whole time.
Common Mistakes

items: Sending the rendered messages straight to the LLM without ever showing them to the user first.
Building a preview that only displays the first message when a prompt actually returns several.
Re calling prompts/get after every keystroke of an edit instead of editing the local copy.
Caching a rendered result as if it were reusable across different argument values.
Showing raw resource identifiers in a preview instead of a readable name or excerpt.
Swallowing a failed prompts/get call silently instead of telling the user what went wrong.

blocks.text: Practice

Write a small client function that takes a prompt name and a raw comma separated slash command input, calls prompts/get, prints the rendered messages for a mock preview, accepts a one line edit from a variable, and then prints the final messages that would be sent to the LLM.
Key Takeaway

Using a prompt is a short pipeline: collect the arguments a user filled in, call prompts/get to have the server render the messages, then let the user see and adjust that text before it ever reaches the LLM.
The preview and edit step is what turns a filled in template into something a user actually trusts, since nothing gets sent to the model without them having seen the exact final wording first.
